sections.desc: Part 1: 59 targeted fixes for your weak patterns (P1–P3). Part 2: 50 breadth Hards (B1 < 2350, B2 ≥ 2350). Hints are spoilers.

x.why: Several of your DP misses needed a faster transition, not a new state. Here the O(m²) row-to-row max collapses to O(m) with two sweeps, a standard trick for late OA questions.
x.hint: left[c] = max(left[c−1] − 1, prev[c]); right[c] = max(right[c+1] − 1, prev[c]); cur[c] = points[r][c] + max(left[c], right[c]).

x.pat: Sort by one key, then weighted LIS on the other
x.why: 1691 is this exact pattern with three dimensions, and 1713 needed the same 'reduce it to LIS' step. Solve this, then redo 1691.
x.hint: Sort by (age, score); dp[i] = score[i] + max dp[j] over j < i with score[j] ≤ score[i]. O(n²) passes; a BIT over scores gives O(n log n).

x.pat: Knapsack counting with a reframed contribution
x.why: 2742 and 805 were knapsacks hidden behind a reframing. Here each element is outside the subsequence, inside but not summed, or summed, and that three-way choice collapses to a 1D knapsack.
x.hint: dp[0] = 1; for each x, for s from k down to 0: dp[s] = 2·dp[s] + (s ≥ x ? dp[s−x] : 0), mod 1e9+7. Answer dp[k].

x.pat: Counting DP: length × distinct songs used
x.why: 3193 and 1866 are counting DPs where the state is a count, not a set. This is the cleanest example of choosing that state.
x.hint: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]·(n−j+1) + dp[i−1][j]·max(j−k, 0). Answer dp[goal][n].

x.pat: DP keyed by value + best of the previous layer
x.why: 3351 needed a DP indexed by value (hash map); 3651 needed the previous layer's best to avoid an inner loop. This problem combines both.
x.hint: f[x][j] = longest ending in value x with ≤ j changes; g[j] = max over all x. For each x, j from k down to 0: f[x][j] = max(f[x][j] + 1, g[j−1] + 1) (g term only if j > 0); then update g[j].

x.why: Your string-DP misses got stuck on making each transition O(1). The fix is to precompute a string fact first, here an LCP table.
x.hint: lcp[i][j] = s[i]==s[j] ? lcp[i+1][j+1] + 1 : 0. dp[i] = max(1, 1 + max dp[i+L] over L with lcp[i][i+L] ≥ L).

x.pat: Kadane over character pairs with a 'must contain' flag
x.why: Amazon-tagged, including recently. It's Kadane with a 'must contain at least one b' condition, the same constrained-Kadane reasoning 3410 needed inside segment-tree nodes.
x.hint: For each ordered pair (a, b): f0 = run with no b yet, f1 = best with ≥ 1 b (start −∞). On a: f0++, f1++. On b: f1 = max(f0, f1) − 1, f0 = 0. Track max f1.

x.pat: Sort both sides, then contiguous-assignment DP
x.why: Like 2742 and 1883, the hard part is spotting the state: after sorting, each factory repairs a contiguous block of robots.
x.hint: dp(i, j) = min(dp(i, j+1), min over t ≤ limit_j of dist(robots i..i+t−1 → factory j) + dp(i+t, j+1)).

x.pat: LIS-style DP + Fenwick prefix max on a transformed key
x.why: Direct follow-up to 2407: rewrite nums[i] − nums[j] ≥ i − j as key[i] = nums[i] − i ≥ key[j], then query the best dp over smaller keys.
x.hint: Compress keys; dp[i] = nums[i] + max(0, BITmax(≤ key[i])). Answer = max dp (an all-negative input gives the max element).

groups.name: 2. Bitmask DP
groups.sub: your misses: 465, 1494, 1723, 1125, 2172, 1349, 1815, 805 + profile DP 1931 (bitmask-tagged: 5 of 13 solved)

x.why: Bridge to 1931 and 1349: enumerate valid row patterns, precompute which can stack, then DP over rows. Afterwards redo 1931 with m ≤ 5.
x.hint: 12 valid rows: 6 'ABA', 6 'ABC'. Next row: ABA' = 3·ABA + 2·ABC, ABC' = 2·ABA + 2·ABC.

x.why: 1723 and 465 are 'partition into groups' bitmask DPs. Learn the O(2ⁿ·n) pair-state trick here (CSES Elevator Rides style) as an alternative to 3ⁿ submask loops.
x.hint: dp[mask] = lexicographically smallest (count, load), dp[0] = (1, 0). Adding task t: if load + t ≤ sessionTime → (c, load + t), else (c + 1, t).

x.why: 2172 and 1125 are assignment DPs. The key trick: the item you're placing is implied by popcount(mask), so the state is just the mask.
x.hint: dp[mask] = min over j in mask of dp[mask ^ (1<<j)] + (a[popcount(mask) − 1] XOR b[j]).

x.why: 864 is a BFS whose state includes a bitmask. Same template on a cleaner graph: learn it here, then redo 864.
x.hint: Push every (i, 1<<i) at distance 0; visited[node][mask]; the first time mask == full, return the distance.

x.pat: Submask enumeration over precomputed valid groups
x.why: The 3ⁿ submask DP behind 465, 1494 and 1723. Precompute the cost of every valid group mask, then DP over submasks.
x.hint: cost[g] for |g| = n/k with distinct values. dp[mask] = min dp[mask ^ g] + cost[g] over valid g ⊆ mask that contain mask's lowest set bit.

x.why: 84, 85 and 2334 all treat each element as the bottleneck of its widest window. This drills the PSE/NSE template plus the tie-break for equal values.
x.hint: ans += a[i]·(i − PSE[i])·(NSE[i] − i). Use strictly-smaller on one side and smaller-or-equal on the other so equal values aren't counted twice.

x.pat: Element as the min of its maximal window + prefix sums
x.why: This is 84 with the width replaced by a range sum, and the same 'each element is the min of its maximal window' view that 2334 needed.
x.hint: Window for i is (PSE, NSE); value = a[i]·(pre[NSE] − pre[PSE + 1]). Maximise in 64-bit and take the mod only at the end.

x.why: 862 needed a monotonic deque over prefix sums. Here the deque sits inside a DP, the standard O(n·k) → O(n) speed-up.
x.hint: dp[i] = nums[i] + max(0, max dp[i−k..i−1]). Keep indices in a deque with decreasing dp; drop the front when its index < i − k.

x.pat: Greedy lexicographic stack with a feasibility check
x.why: 321 = best length-k subsequence via a stack, then a merge. This trains the stack-pop rule with a look-ahead check (last occurrence), which is the core of 321.
x.hint: Skip c if it's already in the stack. Otherwise pop while top > c and top appears again later; then push c.

x.pat: Monotonic-stack range counting + greedy + fast power
x.why: An OA-style composite: sieve the prime scores, count the subarrays where each index is the chosen one, then spend k greedily on the largest values with modpow.
x.hint: count_i = (i − L)·(R − i), L = previous index with score ≥ score[i], R = next index with score > score[i]. Take values in descending order, min(k, count_i) of each.

groups.name: 4. Graphs: Shortest-path Variants, State BFS, DSU, Functional Graphs

x.why: 2493 needed 'BFS from every vertex and reason about levels'. This is the simplest drill of that technique.
x.hint: BFS from each source; on edge (u, v) with v already seen and v ≠ parent[u], cycle = d[u] + d[v] + 1. Take the minimum.

x.pat: Dijkstra + path counting on the shortest-path DAG
x.why: 126 timed out because the shortest-path DAG wasn't used. Counting paths on that DAG during Dijkstra is the cleanest exercise.
x.hint: If d[u] + w < d[v]: update d[v], ways[v] = ways[u]. If equal: ways[v] += ways[u] (mod). Use 64-bit distances.

x.why: 2127 hinged on splitting an out-degree-1 graph into cycles and the trees hanging off them. This is the pure version.
x.hint: Peel indegree-0 nodes (Kahn); what remains are cycles, answer = cycle length. Then, in reverse peel order, ans[u] = 1 + ans[next[u]].

x.pat: Reverse-time DSU with virtual nodes (or BS + BFS)
x.why: Combines 1168's dummy-node trick with the reverse/sorted-order DSU from 2334 and 2421. Solve it both ways.
x.hint: Go backwards through the days turning cells into land; union with land neighbours; row 0 ↔ TOP, last row ↔ BOTTOM. When TOP and BOTTOM connect after restoring cells[d−1], the answer is d − 1.

x.why: 1368 was about choosing the right shortest-path variant for grid costs. Here arrival times are constrained and you can stall by stepping back and forth, a frequent OA twist.
x.hint: If grid[0][1] > 1 and grid[1][0] > 1 → −1. Else from time t you reach v at t + 1 if t + 1 ≥ g[v], otherwise at g[v] + ((g[v] − t − 1) mod 2).

x.pat: 0-1 BFS on a composite state (box, player)
x.why: 864 and 1368 in one problem: the state is (box, player); walking costs 0 and pushing costs 1, so it's a 0-1 BFS.
x.hint: Player steps into a free cell → cost 0 (push_front). Player steps into the box → box moves the same way if free → cost 1 (push_back).

x.why: Two metrics at once (time limit and fee): a step up from the single-extra-state BFS in 1293 and the multi-Dijkstra in 2203.
x.hint: f[t][v] = min fee to be at v at exactly time t (t ≤ maxTime ≤ 1000). For each t relax every edge. Answer = min over t of f[t][n−1].

x.why: 1591 was about building the right dependency graph before the topo sort. Here you build two graphs (groups and items) and nest the orders.
x.hint: Give each ungrouped item its own new group. Edges between groups go to the group graph, edges inside a group to the item graph. Topo-sort both, then output items group by group.

x.why: DSU modelling (2421, 1579) plus number theory (1250): union numbers through shared primes instead of checking O(n²) pairs.
x.hint: Factor each x (SPF sieve or trial division up to √x) and union x with each prime factor. Answer = largest group size counted over the input numbers.

x.pat: Tree DP with two states per node
x.why: You've done the edge-flip kind of rerooting (2858). This one needs path aggregation across children, the harder half of 834.
x.hint: dfs returns (a, b) = best downward path sum ending at a leaf, and the same without that leaf. Merging child (c, d): ans = max(ans, a + d, b + c); then a = max(a, p + c), b = max(b, p + d).

x.why: 2458 needs subtree-removal reasoning with Euler-tour ancestor checks. Here two cut edges give three parts, and an O(1) ancestor test picks the case.
x.hint: Root at 0, sub[x] = subtree XOR. For cut nodes i, j: if i is an ancestor of j → sub[j], sub[i]^sub[j], total^sub[i]; else sub[i], sub[j], total^sub[i]^sub[j].

x.why: The max-based rerooting that 834's technique generalises to: keep the best and second-best downward values so each child can get 'best excluding me' from its parent.
x.hint: Stepping into node v costs 1 if v is odd, 2 if even. Store down1/down2 (and which child gave down1); up[v] = cost(u) + max(up[u], best down of u not through v).

x.pat: LCA via binary lifting + prefix counts on root paths
x.why: You haven't solved an LCA problem yet (1483 is still blank). This adds per-weight counts on paths: the standard f(u) + f(v) − 2·f(lca) query.
x.hint: cnt[v][w] = edges of weight w (1..26) on root→v. Path counts = cnt[u] + cnt[v] − 2·cnt[lca]; answer = path length − max count.

groups.name: 6. Advanced DS: BIT / Segment Tree / Sweep Line / Offline Queries
groups.sub: your misses: 493, 2179, 2659, 3410, 218, 732, 2407 (segment tree 2 of 9 solved, BIT 2 of 7)

x.why: 218 and 732 are sweep-line problems. This is the standard area-union sweep and the prerequisite for 3454 in your blank list.
x.hint: Events (x, y1, y2, ±1) sorted by x; between consecutive x add covered-y-length × Δx. Covered length from cover counts over compressed y (n ≤ 200, so O(n²) is fine).

x.pat: Offline queries + monotonic stack + binary search
x.why: Extends your offline-query wins (2503, 1851) to 'first index to the right taller than X', which a monotonic stack answers.
x.hint: Make a ≤ b. If a == b or h[a] < h[b] → b. Else find the first j > b with h[j] > h[a]: sort queries by b descending, push buildings right-to-left onto a stack of increasing heights, binary-search it.

x.pat: Greedy + Fenwick tree tracking shifted positions
x.why: 2659 needed a BIT to count how far elements shift after earlier removals. Same mechanic, driving a greedy.
x.hint: Queue of positions per digit. At each step take the smallest digit whose front position p costs p − (moved positions < p) ≤ k; subtract the cost and mark p in the BIT.

x.pat: Fix the middle pair, count both sides
x.why: Harder sibling of 2179: fix (j, k) with nums[j] > nums[k], then multiply the counts on the left and right.
x.hint: For j < k with nums[j] > nums[k]: add (#i < j with nums[i] < nums[k]) × (#l > k with nums[l] > nums[j]). Prefix-count tables give O(n²) for n ≤ 4000.

x.pat: Segment tree with a custom merge (prefix/suffix/best)
x.why: 3410 needed exactly this: store prefix run, suffix run and best per node and merge children, with point updates.
x.hint: Node = (len, pre, suf, best, leftChar, rightChar). When merging, join left.suf + right.pre if the boundary characters match.

x.why: Amazon and Goldman Sachs tagged it recently. As in 2968 and 2071, the trick is to search for the cut-off value instead of simulating orders one by one.
x.hint: Find the smallest T with Σ max(0, a − T) ≤ orders. Sell everything above T with arithmetic-series sums, then sell the remaining orders at price T.

x.pat: Binary search with a non-obvious feasibility check
x.why: 2071 and 3049 broke on the check function. Here T is feasible iff Σ min(b, T) ≥ n·T, so practise proving checks like this.
x.hint: hi = Σb / n; check(T): Σ min(b_i, T) ≥ n·T. Use 64-bit.

x.pat: Binary search + greedy with a difference array
x.why: Same shape as 2071: binary-search the target, then greedily place resources as far right as possible, tracked with a sliding difference array.
x.hint: check(T): sweep i with a running add; if power[i] + add < T, put the shortfall at min(n−1, i + r) (covers up to i + 2r); fail if the total exceeds k.

x.why: 719 needed 'binary-search the answer, count fast'. Here the count is pure math (lcm inclusion–exclusion), which also exercises the number theory behind 1250.
x.hint: x works iff x − x/d1 ≥ c1, x − x/d2 ≥ c2 and x − x/lcm(d1, d2) ≥ c1 + c2.

x.why: The same invariant as 330: if you can make every value in [0, r), a coin c ≤ r extends that to [0, r + c).
x.hint: Sort; r = 1; for each coin c: if c > r stop, else r += c. Return r.

x.pat: Regret greedy: commit now, drop the worst later
x.why: 871's idea exactly: take courses greedily, keep their durations in a max-heap, and drop the longest when a deadline breaks.
x.hint: Sort by lastDay; push d, t += d; if t > lastDay: t −= heap.top(), pop.

x.pat: Sort by one key, heap over the other
x.why: Same skeleton as 1383, one level harder: fix the max wage/quality ratio in sorted order and keep the k smallest qualities in a max-heap.
x.hint: Sort by wage/quality; keep sumQ of the k smallest qualities; cost = ratio × sumQ.

x.why: A swap-counting greedy like 765: show that pairing the leftmost character with its rightmost match is optimal.
x.hint: For each left i: find the rightmost k ≤ j with s[k] == s[i] and bubble it to j (add j − k, then j−−). If s[i] has no partner (the odd middle char), add n/2 − i and move on.

x.pat: Interval greedy: place points at right ends
x.why: Interval/greedy is on your OA list. You've done DP on intervals (1235, 1751) but not point-hitting greedy with multiplicity.
x.hint: Sort by end asc, start desc. Keep the last two chosen points p1 < p2; for each interval add 0, 1 (at end) or 2 (end − 1, end) points as needed.

x.why: Candy-style two passes (135) at a harder level: push limits left-to-right and right-to-left, then compute the peak between each pair of restrictions.
x.hint: Add (1, 0) and sort. h[i] = min(h[i], h[i−1] + Δ), then the same backwards. Peak between = (h1 + h2 + Δ)/2; also check the tail up to n.

groups.name: 9. Math: Combinatorics, Number Theory, Bits
groups.sub: your misses: 3405, 1250, 1866, 3193, 1611, 780 (bit manipulation 10 of 22 solved)

x.pat: nCr mod p with factorial + inverse factorial
x.why: 3405 stalled on nCr and the modular inverse. Build fact/invFact once (Fermat); every OA combinatorics question reuses this template.
x.hint: Sort. a[i] is the max in Σ_{j<k} C(i, j) subsequences and the min in Σ_{j<k} C(n−1−i, j).

x.pat: At most ~30 distinct ORs end at each index
x.why: Bit manipulation is one of your weakest tags. The 'OR/AND over subarrays changes at most log V times' trick comes up often in OAs.
x.hint: Keep the set S of ORs of subarrays ending at i: S' = {x | a[i] : x in S} ∪ {a[i]} (≤ 30 values). Check |k − v| for each.

x.pat: Reduce to gcd buckets (divisors of k)
x.why: 1250 was gcd reasoning. Map x → gcd(x, k); only divisors of k matter (at most 128 of them), so you pair buckets instead of numbers.
x.hint: cnt[g] for g = gcd(x, k). For bucket pairs with g1·g2 % k == 0 add cnt[g1]·cnt[g2] (g1 < g2) or C(cnt[g], 2) (g1 == g2).

x.pat: Binary trie with deletions + sliding window
x.why: Step up from 1707 (offline XOR trie): now the candidate set slides (y ≤ 2x after sorting), so the trie needs counts to support removal.
x.hint: Sort. For y = a[r]: remove a[l] while 2·a[l] < y, insert y, query the max XOR with y.

x.pat: Orderings of a tree = n! / Π subtree sizes
x.why: Combinatorial counting (3193, 3405) on a tree: derive the multinomial formula, then reuse the modular-inverse template from 3428.
x.hint: ans = n! · Π inv(size[v]) mod 1e9+7. Use an iterative DFS (n ≤ 1e5).

x.why: 2851 needed Z/KMP for rotation matching. You know KMP (214, 3008); add the Z-function to your templates, since it's a one-liner here.
x.hint: Answer = n + Σ z[i] for i ≥ 1.

x.why: 336 (and 745 in your blank list) match prefixes and suffixes together. A pair-keyed trie checks both in one walk.
x.hint: For each word, walk the trie on keys (w[i], w[n−1−i]) adding end-counts along the path; then insert the word and increment its end node.

x.pat: Trie of reversed words over a stream
x.why: 642 and 527 were trie designs. Insert words reversed; each query walks the trie from the newest character backwards.
x.hint: Keep the last maxLen characters. On query, walk from the newest char backwards; return true at the first word end, false at a missing child.

x.pat: Ordered set of free indices + lazy cleanup
x.why: 1606 needed a 'set of free indices, take the leftmost' structure. Same invariant here, plus pop-from-the-right bookkeeping.
x.hint: Min-heap (or set) of non-full stack indices. push → smallest valid index; pop → trim empty stacks from the right first; popAtStack(i) → add i back to the free set.

x.pat: Interval set in an ordered map (split and merge)
x.why: Builds on your interval set from 2276 by adding range removal, the interval splitting that 732 also relies on.
x.hint: map<start, end>. add: merge everything overlapping; remove: cut overlapping intervals into left/right pieces; query: upper_bound, step back, check containment.

groups.name: 12. Sliding Window: Step-ups Only
groups.sub: your strongest area (15 of 17 solved), so only harder variants

x.why: Your strongest area, so only step-ups: shrink the window by checking suffixes of length ≤ 10 against a hash set.
x.hint: For each right end r, check word[i..r] for i from r down to max(l, r − 9); if one is forbidden, set l = i + 1.

x.pat: Binary search + count subarrays with ≤ d distinct
x.why: Builds on the at-most-k window (992, still blank) and pairs it with binary search, a two-technique combo typical of a last OA question.
x.hint: m = n(n+1)/2. Find the smallest d with count(subarrays with ≤ d distinct) ≥ (m + 1)/2.

groups.name: 13. DP: New State Types
groups.sub: two-state, value-state + binary search, insertion DP, hashmap per index, automaton, bitset, sort-by-value

x.why: The only choice per index is swap or keep, and validity depends only on the previous pair. Teaches compressing 2ⁿ choices into two rolling states, a common OA DP shape.
x.hint: keep/swap = min swaps with index i kept/swapped. If a[i]>a[i−1] and b[i]>b[i−1]: keep ← keep, swap ← swap+1. If a[i]>b[i−1] and b[i]>a[i−1]: keep ← min(keep, swap), swap ← min(swap, keep+1).

x.pat: DP over the last value + binary search in a sorted pool
x.why: When replacements come from a sorted pool, the state becomes 'last value used', and only the smallest pool value above it matters (upper_bound).
x.hint: Sort and dedupe arr2. dp = map {last value → min ops}. For each a, from (v, c): if a > v keep (a, c); also b = upper_bound(arr2, v) gives (b, c + 1). Keep the min cost per value.

x.pat: Permutation DP by relative rank (insertion) + prefix sums
x.why: 3193 and 629 both count permutations by building them one element at a time. Here the state is the rank of the last element among those placed, and prefix sums make it O(n²).
x.hint: f[i][j] = ways for the first i characters ending at rank j of i + 1 values. 'D': f[i][j] = Σ_{k ≥ j} f[i−1][k]; 'I': f[i][j] = Σ_{k < j} f[i−1][k]. Use prefix sums.

x.pat: dp[i][diff] with a hashmap per index
x.tgt: New: your diff-state DP (956) used a bounded array
x.why: When the state value (a difference) is unbounded, give each index its own hashmap. Counting 'weak' length-2 sequences avoids a separate length dimension.
x.hint: For j < i, d = a[i] − a[j] (64-bit): ans += f[j][d]; f[i][d] += f[j][d] + 1.

x.why: Digit DP where the extra state is 'how much of the forbidden word is matched', advanced with KMP failure links. The template for any 'count strings avoiding a pattern' question.
x.hint: dfs(pos, matched, tightLow, tightHigh); next matched via KMP transitions; matched == |evil| → 0. Memoise; or compute count(≤ s2) − count(< s1).

x.why: When a boolean knapsack is too slow, a bitset updates 64 sums per word. After sorting, value v can only be added to totals below v, so each step is a masked shift.
x.hint: Sort unique values; f = 1; for each v: f |= (f & ((1 << v) − 1)) << v (std::bitset). Answer = highest set bit.

x.pat: Process cells in value order; DP via row/column best
x.why: With up to 1e5 cells the move graph is too dense for DFS. Sort by value and keep the best length per row and column, handling equal values as a batch.
x.hint: Group cells by value ascending. For a group, compute f = 1 + max(rowBest[r], colBest[c]) for every cell first, then write all rowBest/colBest updates.

groups.name: 14. Game Theory & Probability
groups.sub: minimax DP, game DP with prefix sums, probability by counting

x.tgt: New: 810 was a brainteaser, not a DP
x.why: Most OA game problems reduce to 'current player maximises (what I take − opponent's best on the rest)'. This is the one-line recurrence to learn.
x.hint: f[i] = max over x = 1..3 of (sum(i..i+x−1) − f[i+x]), filled from the right. The sign of f[0] decides Alice, Bob or Tie.

x.pat: Game DP collapsed with prefix sums + a running max
x.why: Merging piles leaves the prefix sums unchanged, so each move is just picking a cut. The game DP then becomes a running max from the right.
x.hint: pre = prefix sums; f = pre[n−1]; for i from n−2 down to 1: f = max(f, pre[i] − f). Answer f.

x.pat: Probability = favourable / total by combinatorial counting
x.why: OA probability questions are usually counting in disguise. Enumerate how many balls of each colour go to box 1 and weight each choice by a binomial.
x.hint: Total = C(2n, n). dfs(colour, takenInBox1, distinctDiff) multiplying C(balls[i], x); add states where taken == n and diff == 0; divide by the total.

groups.name: 15. Math: Counting & Number Theory
groups.sub: stars and bars, Stirling numbers, gcd counting, prime-factor intervals, prime masks, permutation counting

x.pat: Stars and bars over prime exponents
x.why: Spreading a prime's exponent x over n slots is C(x + n − 1, n − 1), and different primes are independent. Standard for 'count arrays with a given product' questions.
x.hint: Precompute fact/invFact up to ~1e4 + 20. Factor k; ans = Π C(x_p + n − 1, n − 1) mod 1e9+7.

x.pat: Stirling numbers of the second kind (DP)
x.why: Counting ways to split people into exactly j non-empty groups, then labelling the groups, is a building block for many counting questions.
x.hint: f[i][j] = f[i−1][j]·j + f[i−1][j−1]·(x − j + 1). Answer Σ_j f[n][j]·y^j.

x.pat: Pairs with gcd exactly g via multiples (subtract from large g down)
x.why: Pairs whose gcd is a multiple of g number C(m_g, 2); subtract the exact counts for 2g, 3g, … (harmonic loop). Prefix sums plus binary search then answer 'k-th gcd' queries.
x.hint: m_g = count of multiples of g; exact[g] = C(m_g, 2) − Σ_{t ≥ 2} exact[t·g], for g from max down. Prefix-sum exact[], upper_bound each query.

x.why: A coprime split means no prime appears on both sides. Each prime spans [first, last]; the answer is the first index where the running max of right ends stops.
x.hint: Factor every number; last[p] = last index of p. For i: reach = max(reach, last[p] for p | nums[i]); if reach == i and i < n − 1 → answer i.

x.tgt: New: masks over primes, not positions
x.why: Values ≤ 30 use at most 10 distinct primes, so the state is a prime mask. Values divisible by a square are skipped, and 1s multiply the count by 2^(#ones).
x.hint: f[0] = 1; for x in 2..30 (skip if divisible by 4, 9 or 25) with cnt[x] > 0: for masks descending containing mask_x: f[mask] += f[mask ^ mask_x]·cnt[x]. Answer (Σ_{mask ≠ 0} f)·2^cnt[1].

x.pat: Enumerate palindromes by first half + count multiset permutations
x.why: Generate only ~10^5 palindromes, keep those divisible by k, dedupe by sorted digits, and count arrangements without a leading zero.
x.hint: Per digit multiset: (n − c0)·(n − 1)! / Π c_d!. Use the sorted digit string as the dedupe key.

x.pat: Sort + contribution with a doubling running sum
x.why: Subset problems where only the max and min matter: sort, fix one end, and keep a running sum whose weights double each step.
x.hint: Sort ascending. p = 0; for x: ans += x²·(x + p); p = 2p + x (all mod 1e9+7).

groups.name: 16. Math Techniques: Matrix Power & Convex Search
groups.sub: linear recurrences with huge t, convex cost with no closed form

x.pat: Matrix exponentiation of a linear recurrence
x.why: When t is up to 1e9, write one step as a 26×26 transition matrix and raise it to the t-th power in O(26³ log t). The same tool cracks 2851.
x.hint: M[i][j] = 1 if letter i turns into letter j (j in i+1..i+nums[i], mod 26). Answer = sum of (count vector × M^t).

x.pat: Convex optimisation: nested ternary search / gradient descent
x.why: The sum of Euclidean distances is convex, so nested ternary search (x outside, y inside) or gradient descent converges. Useful whenever a cost is convex but has no closed form.
x.hint: Ternary search x in [0, 100]; for each x ternary search y; about 100 iterations each reaches 1e-5 precision.

groups.name: 17. Bits & Masks: Submasks, AND/XOR Counting, BIT Greedy
groups.sub: hashing masks, value-domain counting, XOR trie counting, per-bit greedy

x.pat: Enumerate submasks of each query + hashmap of word masks
x.tgt: New: your submask work so far is DP, not hashing
x.why: Each puzzle has 7 letters, so only 2^7 submasks. Count word masks in a map, then sum the counts over submasks that contain the first letter.
x.hint: cnt[mask(word)]++. For each puzzle: for (sub = rest; ; sub = (sub − 1) & rest) { total += cnt[sub | firstBit]; if (!sub) break; }.

x.pat: Count over the value domain instead of over tuples
x.why: n³ triples are too slow, but values are below 2^16: count every pairwise AND, then pair each AND result with every z.
x.hint: cnt[x & y]++ for all ordered pairs (n²). ans = Σ over v with cnt[v] > 0, Σ over z of cnt[v]·[v & z == 0].

x.pat: Binary trie counting pairs with XOR < K
x.why: Instead of maximising XOR, walk the trie along K's bits and add whole subtrees where K has a 1. count(≤ high) − count(< low) handles ranges.
x.hint: f(x, K): at bit b, if K_b = 1: add size(child with bit x_b) and go to child x_b ^ 1; else go to child x_b. Query each x before inserting it.

x.why: AND/OR operations only move 1-bits between numbers, so count ones per bit and greedily build the k largest numbers. A recurring bitwise OA trick.
x.hint: cnt[b] = ones at bit b. Repeat k times: x = Σ 2^b over bits with cnt[b] > 0 (decrement each); ans += x² mod 1e9+7.

groups.name: 18. Graphs: New Models
groups.sub: Floyd–Warshall, bounded-answer insight, second-shortest path, degree counting, BFS with skip sets

x.tgt: New: no all-pairs shortest path in your sheet
x.why: n ≤ 10, so try every set of kept nodes and run Floyd–Warshall on it. Floyd is the go-to for all-pairs distances when n is small.
x.hint: For each mask: d = INF with the lightest edge between kept nodes; run Floyd; valid if every d[i][j] ≤ maxDistance for i, j in mask.

x.why: A corner can always be cut off in 2 days, so only test 0 and 1 (remove each land cell and recount, or use articulation points). Spotting a small bounded answer is a strong OA trick.
x.hint: If islands ≠ 1 → 0. For each land cell: set it to water and count islands; if ≠ 1 → 1. Otherwise 2.

x.pat: Second-shortest path: keep two distances per node
x.why: Keep the best and strictly second-best arrival per node during BFS; this generalises to k-th shortest. Then convert the hop count to time with the traffic-light rule.
x.hint: d1[v], d2[v] in hops; push (v, d) if d < d1[v] or d1[v] < d < d2[v]. Time: per hop, if (t / change) is odd, wait to the next multiple of change, then t += time.

x.pat: Degree counting + two pointers + shared-edge correction
x.why: Count pairs with deg[a] + deg[b] − shared(a, b) > q: count with sorted degrees and two pointers, then fix only the pairs that actually share edges.
x.hint: Two pointers on sorted degrees count deg sum > q. For each connected pair with multiplicity c: if deg[a] + deg[b] > q and deg[a] + deg[b] − c ≤ q, subtract 1.

x.pat: BFS that skips visited cells with ordered sets
x.why: Each cell reaches a whole row/column range, so naive BFS is O(nm(n+m)). Keep unvisited cells per row and per column in ordered sets so each cell is processed once.
x.hint: BFS from (0,0). For a cell, take unvisited columns in (j, j + g] from rowSet[i] with lower_bound and erase them as you push; same for rows via colSet[j].

groups.name: 19. Trees: New Techniques
groups.sub: path counting via components, usage counts + tree DP, degree-limited DP, parity reduction, subtree mex, equal-sum cuts

x.pat: Count paths through special nodes via component sizes
x.why: Paths with exactly one prime: union the non-prime nodes into components, then for each prime combine the sizes of its neighbouring components.
x.hint: Sieve; union edges whose ends are both non-prime. For prime p with neighbour component sizes c1..ck: ans += Σ ci + Σ_{i<j} ci·cj (running sum).

x.pat: Count node usage, then tree DP (no two adjacent halved)
x.why: Split it into two questions: count how often each node is used over all trips, then run a house-robber DP on the tree to choose which nodes to halve.
x.hint: cnt[v] from a DFS path per trip. dfs(u) returns (full, half): full = cnt·price + Σ min(childFull, childHalf); half = cnt·price/2 + Σ childFull.

x.pat: Degree-limited tree DP: keep the top positive gains
x.why: Each node keeps at most k edges. Every child offers a gain from keeping its edge; take the best positive gains, k of them normally and k − 1 when the parent edge is kept.
x.hint: dfs(u) → (a, b): best with ≤ k child edges, and with ≤ k − 1. Base = Σ child.a; gain = w + child.b − child.a; sort gains descending and add the positive ones.

x.pat: Reduce tree operations to a parity constraint
x.why: XOR-ing every edge on a path flips only its two endpoints, so any even-sized set of nodes can be flipped. The tree disappears; use a two-state parity DP.
x.hint: f0/f1 = best sum with an even/odd number of flips: f0' = max(f0 + x, f1 + (x ^ k)), f1' = max(f1 + x, f0 + (x ^ k)). Answer f0.

x.pat: Subtree mex: only the path from the node with value 1 matters
x.why: Values are distinct, so every subtree without value 1 has mex 1. Walk from that node up to the root, adding each new subtree's values once, with a monotone mex pointer.
x.hint: Find the node with gene 1. For u on the path upward: DFS-add unseen genes of u's subtree to has[]; while has[mex]: mex++; ans[u] = mex. Every other node gets 1.

x.pat: Enumerate the target sum (divisors of total) + greedy cut DFS
x.why: If all components have equal sum t, t divides the total. Try each candidate; a DFS cuts a subtree as soon as its sum reaches t and fails if it goes over.
x.hint: s = Σ nums; for k from n down to 1 with s % k == 0 and s/k ≥ max: dfs returns subtree sum, 0 if it equals t, −1 if above. Root returns 0 → answer k − 1.

groups.name: 20. Advanced DS: Lazy Segment Tree, 2D Offline, BIT Tricks, Majority, K-BEST
groups.sub: range updates, dominance queries, indicator BITs, majority candidates, keeping only k best

x.pat: Lazy segment tree (range flip, range sum)
x.tgt: New: your segment trees so far are point-update
x.why: The standard lazy-propagation template: a pending flip turns a node's sum into length − sum. Everything else is a running total.
x.hint: Node stores the count of ones; flip(l, r): mark lazy and set ones = len − ones; push lazy down before recursing. Type 2: total2 += p·ones(root).

x.pat: Offline 2D dominance: sort one coordinate, BIT on the other
x.why: 'Max over points with x ≥ X and y ≥ Y' is a 2D dominance query: sort points and queries by x descending, insert into a prefix-max BIT keyed by compressed y.
x.hint: Sort points by nums1 desc and queries by x desc; insert points with nums1 ≥ x; the BIT over reversed compressed nums2 stores max(nums1 + nums2); query y.

x.pat: BIT over a 0/1 indicator with local updates
x.why: Many 'count positions with property P in a range, with point updates' questions become a BIT over an indicator where an update only touches nearby indices.
x.hint: peak[i] = a[i−1] < a[i] > a[i+1]. Query (l, r) → sum over l+1..r−1. Update i: remove flags at i−1, i, i+1, assign, add them back.

x.pat: Majority queries: candidate (Boyer–Moore merge) + verify with positions
x.why: Segment-tree nodes merge Boyer–Moore (candidate, count) pairs; then binary-search the candidate's index list to count it. Warm-up for 3636 in your blank list.
x.hint: merge((x, c1), (y, c2)) = x == y ? (x, c1 + c2) : c1 ≥ c2 ? (x, c1 − c2) : (y, c2 − c1). Verify: upper_bound − lower_bound on pos[x] ≥ threshold.

x.pat: Keep only the k best partial results (k-truncation)
x.tgt: New: you solved k-th via binary search (668, 2040)
x.why: When k is small, merge row by row and keep only the k smallest sums. A general trick for k-best over products of choices.
x.hint: pre = [0]; for each row: pre = smallest k of {p + x : p in pre, x in row[:k]}. Answer pre[k−1].

groups.name: 21. Stack & Greedy Variants
groups.sub: second greater, reverse simulation, forced greedy flips, interval closure

x.pat: Second greater element: two monotonic stacks
x.why: Elements waiting for their first greater sit in stack 1; once found they move, order kept, to stack 2, where the next greater element is their answer.
x.hint: For x = a[i]: pop s2 while a[top] < x → ans[top] = x. Pop s1 while a[top] < x into tmp; push i onto s1; push tmp onto s2 in reverse pop order.

x.pat: Reverse the process + max-heap + modulo jumps
x.why: Forward you can't tell which index grew; backwards the max must be the last write. Undo it with modulo rather than repeated subtraction, exactly what 780 needed.
x.hint: total = Σ; pop max mx, rest = total − mx. If mx == 1 or rest == 1 → true. If rest == 0 or mx ≤ rest or mx % rest == 0 → false. Push mx % rest; total = rest + mx % rest.

x.why: The leftmost 0 can only be fixed by a flip starting there, so the greedy is forced; a difference array (or queue) tracks active flips in O(1).
x.hint: cur = parity of active flips; at i: cur ^= endFlip[i]; if a[i] ^ cur == 0: if i + k > n → −1; else cur ^= 1, endFlip[i + k] ^= 1, ans++.

x.pat: Close character intervals, then interval-scheduling greedy
x.why: A valid substring must contain every occurrence of its letters, so expand [first[c], last[c]] until it is closed, then pick non-overlapping intervals greedily by right end.
x.hint: For each c from first[c]: r = last[c]; scan j in [first[c], r], r = max(r, last[s[j]]), invalid if first[s[j]] < first[c]. Sort valid intervals by r and take greedily.

groups.name: 22. Strings & Hashing
groups.sub: occurrence contribution, prefix/suffix matching, √-length hashing DP, binary search + rolling hash, grouping, corner hashing, fixed-window enumeration

x.pat: Contribution via previous/next occurrence of the same character
x.why: A character counts in a substring iff the substring covers it but not its same-letter neighbours, so its contribution is (i − prev)·(next − i). The same trick solves 2262 and many string-sum OA questions.
x.hint: For each letter keep its index list with sentinels −1 and n; ans += (pos[k] − pos[k−1])·(pos[k+1] − pos[k]).

x.pat: Prefix/suffix subsequence matching + two pointers / binary search
x.why: Deleting a middle block of t leaves a prefix and a suffix that must match s from the left and right. Precompute both match arrays and combine them, a standard OA string decomposition.
x.hint: pre[i] = earliest index in s matching t[0..i]; suf[j] = latest index matching t[j..]. Minimise j − i − 1 over pairs with pre[i] < suf[j] (two pointers or binary search on length).

x.pat: DP + rolling hash over the distinct word lengths only (√ trick)
x.why: Total word length ≤ 5e4 means at most ~316 distinct lengths. At each position try only those lengths, checking substrings by hash: O(n√L) instead of O(n·L).
x.hint: best[(len, hash)] = min cost. f[0] = 0; f[i] = min over distinct lengths ℓ ≤ i of f[i − ℓ] + best[(ℓ, hash(t[i−ℓ..i)))]. Use double hashing.

x.pat: Binary search on length + rolling-hash sets
x.why: Feasibility is monotone in length, so binary-search it and check with rolling hashes of every window across paths. 1044 in your blank list is the easier warm-up.
x.hint: check(L): hashes of all length-L windows in path 0, intersected with each next path's set; non-empty → feasible. Use double hashing to avoid collisions.

x.pat: Group by first letter; count with 26×26 intersections
x.why: Two ideas can swap first letters iff neither new word exists, which depends only on suffix overlaps between the two letter groups.
x.hint: S[c] = set of suffixes for first letter c. For c1 < c2: k = |S[c1] ∩ S[c2]|; ans += 2·(|S[c1]| − k)·(|S[c2]| − k).

x.why: A perfect tiling has total area equal to the bounding box, and every corner except the four outer ones appears an even number of times. Hashing corners turns geometry into counting.
x.hint: Sum the areas; toggle each rectangle's 4 corners in a set. At the end the set must be exactly the 4 bounding-box corners, and the areas must match.

x.pat: Enumerate the number of distinct letters → fixed-length window
x.why: Windows where each letter appears exactly k times have length d·k for d distinct letters (≤ 26). Fixing d makes the window length fixed; first split where adjacent letters differ by more than 2.
x.hint: Split s where |s[i] − s[i−1]| > 2. In each part, for d = 1..26 slide a window of length d·k and count windows where exactly d letters have frequency k.
